name: Fading affect bias
statement: The emotion attached to an unpleasant personal memory fades faster over time than the emotion attached to a pleasant one.
meaning: The bias is a difference between two difference scores. A person names an autobiographical event, rates how pleasant or unpleasant it felt at the time, and rates how it feels now. Subtracting one rating from the other gives the fading for that event. The fading affect bias is the finding that this drop is larger for unpleasant events than for pleasant ones. It is a claim about emotion rather than about recall. Walker and Skowronski report that in the founding studies participants remembered positive and negative events with almost equal clarity while their emotions diverged. Ritchie and colleagues later split the outcome four ways: affect that stays fixed, fades, grows more intense, or flips valence. Only the second is fading in the literal sense, and the bias is a pattern across all four.

origin.who: W. Richard Walker, Rodney J. Vogl and Charles P. Thompson
origin.where: Applied Cognitive Psychology, volume 11, issue 5, pages 399-413
origin.note: Three diary studies in which participants recorded unique events and rated their pleasantness as they happened, then rated the same events again in the laboratory after 3.5 months, one year or 4.5 years. Walker and Skowronski's 2009 review calls this paper the start of the modern era of the effect and names two earlier sightings it builds on, Cason in 1932 and Holmes in 1970. The 1997 full text was not obtained, so everything stated about its design here is read off that review.

evidence: Walker and Skowronski summarise the 1997 diary data as two trends: longer retention intervals produced more fading, and unpleasant affect faded more than pleasant affect at every interval. Their account of the sample is not self consistent, giving 38 participants at the 3.5-month interval in the text and 43 in the caption of the figure that plots it. Independent laboratories have since produced the same asymmetry with much larger samples. Marsh, Hammond and Crawford collected 2,368 memories from 296 students at Victoria University of Wellington, half positive and half negative, rated on a scale from -3 to +3 at occurrence and at recall. Positive affect faded less than negative affect, with a multilevel coefficient of -0.680 and a 95% interval from -0.743 to -0.617. Gibbons and four colleagues ran the same comparison on 284 in-person and 157 online participants at an American university. In the in-person study the mean drop was 0.050 scale points for pleasant events against 2.001 for unpleasant ones, F(1, 2116) = 1048.833, p < 0.001, partial eta squared 0.331. Hoehne and Zimprich took 12,314 memories from 2,163 German-speaking adults aged 18 to 98. Scoring change from the rating difference, 39.7% of negative memories faded against 14.8% of positive ones. Scoring it from what participants said had happened to the memory, the figures were 30.5% and 10.3%. Ritchie and seven colleagues report the bias in each of 10 cultural samples, drawn from more than 2,400 event descriptions by 562 participants.

replication.headline: The asymmetry turns up in every large sample that has looked for it, including 10 cultural samples and independent laboratories in New Zealand, Germany and the United Kingdom, though its size varies with who is tested.
replication.detail: Marsh, Hammond and Crawford's study is the cleanest independent test with a published interval. Their multilevel model of 2,368 memories from 296 participants gives an unstandardised coefficient of -0.680 for the valence difference in fading, 95% interval -0.743 to -0.617, p < 0.001, on the study's own -3 to +3 rating scale. Hitchcock and six colleagues found the bias in both of two clinical groups at Cambridge. It gave d = 2.14 in 23 never-depressed adults and d = 1.08 in 21 adults diagnosed with major depressive disorder by structured interview. The gap between the groups gave F(1, 40) = 6.97, p = 0.01, partial eta squared 0.15. Hoehne and Zimprich found it in 12,314 German-language memories by two different scoring methods. Ritchie and colleagues found it in all 10 of their cultural samples. Walker was an author of that paper and of the 1997 original, so it broadens the founding group's work rather than testing it from outside. Muir, Brown and Madill at Leeds found that disclosure to an unresponsive listener made unpleasant memories more intense rather than less, which moves the effect rather than removing it.

study.cite: Marsh, C., Hammond, M. D., & Crawford, M. T. (2019). Thinking about negative life events as a mediator between depression and fading affect bias. PLOS ONE, 14(1), e0211147.

limits: Depression is the documented boundary, and it is narrower than it is usually reported to be. Walker, Skowronski, Gibbons, Vogl and Thompson divided participants by Beck Depression Inventory score and found the bias in the non-dysphoric group and not in the dysphoric one, whose pleasant and unpleasant emotions faded at the same rate. Their first study had 19 dysphoric and 46 non-dysphoric participants and their second had 337, and both are described here from Walker and Skowronski's review rather than from the 2003 paper, whose full text was not obtained. Two later studies with clinical measurement weaken the claim. Hitchcock and colleagues found the bias attenuated but present in diagnosed major depression. Marsh, Hammond and Crawford found that higher Beck scores predicted less fading of affect overall, coefficient -0.010 with a 95% interval from -0.016 to -0.004. The interaction with memory valence, which is the bias itself, was flat. It came to 0.001, with an interval from -0.006 to 0.008 and p = 0.722. Anxiety behaves the same way. Walker, Yancu and Skowronski report anxiety by valence interactions in three samples of 98, 50 and 25 participants, with higher anxiety reducing fading for both valences. Method is a live worry. Most studies ask for the original emotion at the moment of recall, so both ratings come from one sitting, and Walker and Skowronski name retrospective bias as the standing criticism that the diary studies were run to answer. Three things could not be checked. The 1997 paper is closed at the publisher and no open copy was found through Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Europe PMC or the authors' own pages. The only open copy of Ritchie and colleagues' 10-culture study sits behind a Cloudflare challenge at Aarhus University, so which cultures were sampled and how large each sample was are not stated here. Gibbons and colleagues' report of their own initial-intensity means contradicts the sentence describing them, so only their fading results are quoted.
misreadings: The fading affect bias and rosy retrospection are separate claims with separate evidence, and quoting one for the other is the commonest error. Rosy retrospection compares three evaluations of a single event, taken before it, during it and after it, and needs momentary ratings collected in the field. The fading affect bias compares the intensity of emotion at an event with the intensity of emotion at recall, across pleasant and unpleasant events, and needs no field measurement at all. One asks whether a holiday is remembered as better than it felt. The other asks whether the sting leaves faster than the glow. The second error is the flat statement that depressed people show no fading affect bias. That result belongs to one 2003 study using a questionnaire cutoff for dysphoria. Hitchcock and colleagues, testing people diagnosed by structured interview, found the bias reduced by roughly half and still reliable at d = 1.08. Third, the bias is often read as a claim that most memories soften. Hoehne and Zimprich found fixed affect the commonest outcome for both valences, with 62.0% of positive and 47.9% of negative memories reported as unchanged. Fourth, people's own beliefs about the process run the other way. Crawford and Marsh asked participants to predict how affect fades. They expected positive events to fade more in the short term and negative events to fade more in the long term. That is not the pattern the data show.
